How Tide Pools Survive Winter

By Mara Lindqvist · October 14, 2026

Every winter the rocky shore turns hostile. Spray freezes on the rocks, storms rearrange the boulders and the sun barely clears the horizon. Yet when spring arrives, the pools are full of life again. Researchers have spent a decade working out how that happens, and the answer is a mix of chemistry, behaviour and luck.

Antifreeze in the blood

Many tide pool snails and barnacles load their tissues with sugars and amino acids that lower the freezing point of their body fluids. A periwinkle can survive with most of the water outside its cells frozen solid, provided the ice never forms inside them. The trick is to let ice form slowly, where it does the least harm.

Hiding in the deep pools

Fish such as blennies retreat to the deepest pools, where the water stays liquid even when the air drops far below zero. Crabs wedge themselves under boulders. Anemones pull in their tentacles and wait. Each of these strategies buys time until the next tide brings warmer sea water back over the rocks.
